This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $t_k(n)$ denote the least $m$ such that\[n\mid m(m+1)(m+2)\cdots (m+k-1).\]Is it true that\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{x^2}{(\log x)^c}\]for some $c>0$?
Is it true that, for $k\geq 2$,\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_{k+1}(n) =o\left(\sum_{n\leq x}t_k(n)\right)?\]
#394: [ErHa78,p.16][ErGr80,p.76]
number theory
In [ErGr80] they mention a conjecture of Erdős that the sum is $o(x^2)$. This was proved by Erdős and Hall [ErHa78], who proved that in fact\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}x^2.\]Erdős and Hall conjecture that the sum is $o(x^2/(\log x)^c)$ for any $c<\log 2$.
Since $t_2(p)=p-1$ for prime $p$ it is trivial that\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\gg \frac{x^2}{\log x}.\]Erdős and Hall [ErHa78] also note that $t_{n-1}(n!)=2$ and $t_{n-2}(n!)\ll n$, which $n=2^r$ shows is the best possible. They ask about the behaviour of $t_{n-3}(n!)$ and also ask ask whether, for infinitely many $n$,\[t_k(n!)< t_{k-1}(n!)-1\]for all $1\leq k<n$. They proved (with Selfridge) that this holds for $n=10$.
Additional thanks to: Sarosh Adenwalla, Stijn Cambie, Zachary Chase, and Wouter van Doorn

A partial proof 
claimed by Jeff Pickhardt and Omniscience Research Agent (using Omniscience Research Agent).
 Summary:
 We have $$\sum_{n \le x} t_2(n) \gg \frac{x^2}{(\log x)^{1/2}\log \log x}.$$ Since m and m+1 are coprime, splitting n = a·b (coprime) forces a | m and b | m+1, and each such splitting gives one candidate m. So t₂(n) is the smallest over all 2^ω(n) coprime splittings, and each candidate's size is controlled by a modular inverse a⁻¹ mod b. t₂(n) is large only when all those inverses simultaneously avoid the top of their ranges. Controlling many modular inverses at once, over a sparse set of n, is a hard equidistribution problem with no known unconditional handle.
Key trick: engineer n so the inverses become congruences. Instead of taking arbitrary n, build n = a·b with a prime and b squarefree. Then every one of the 2^ω(n) splitting conditions collapses into a plain congruence condition on a, modulo a divisor of b. Note that the map is a bijection. So "is this inverse in the middle of its range?" becomes "is a in this set of residue classes mod b?" No equidistribution needed.
 Notes:
 Colin Snyder / Starfleet's solution shows that the sum is $\ll x^2 (\log x)^{-c}$ with $c = \frac{1}{2048}$. Our complementary lower bound shows that you cannot take $c > \frac{1}{2}$. In particular, the strong conjecture that it holds for all $c < \log 2$ is false. This stronger conjecture is also mentioned in the Formal Conjectures project by Google Deepmind (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/394.lean, line 75).

A full proof 
claimed by Colin Snyder (using GPT 5.6 (custom harness)).
 Summary:
 For $t_k(n)$ the least positive $m$ with $n\mid m(m+1)\cdots(m+k-1)$, we claim both answers are yes:\[\sum_{n\le x}t_2(n)\ll\frac{x^2}{(\log x)^c}\ \text{with explicit }c=\tfrac{1}{2048},\\ \sum_{n\le x}t_{k+1}(n)=o!\left(\sum_{n\le x}t_k(n)\right)\ \text{for every fixed }k\ge2.\]Proved in Lean 4 / Mathlib, standard axioms only, no sorry.
Idea: primes force $t_k(p)=p+1-k$, so the saving only exists on average. An explicit finite Brun sieve over medium primes bounds the $t_{k+1}$ sum, while attaching one large prime to each selected modulus gives a lower bound for the $t_k$ sum with an extra Euler factor $\prod_p(1+\tfrac1{Kp})$. The two Euler products obey an exact powered gap, $(A/E)^M\le B^{M+1}$, and carrying that identity intact converts the extra power into the logarithmic separation. A dense grid $X_N=16^N$ then upgrades the estimate to every real cutoff, not just a subsequence.
 Notes:
 Verify: unzip (106 Lean files), run the included verifier; "#print axioms" on the two final theorems gives exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. The constant $c=1/2048$ is explicit in the formal statement, and the little-o conclusion is stated with Mathlib's IsLittleO over all real cutoffs.
